column2: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Single-nucleus RNA sequencing compared cellular responses in 5XFAD mice and human Alzheimer's disease tissue, including the effects of TREM2 variation. Mouse data identified disease-associated microglia and a reactive oligodendrocyte population. Human glial responses differed substantially from those in mice and implicated altered immune activity, myelination and metabolic support. TREM2 risk variants were associated with weaker microglial reactive programs, supporting a role for TREM2 while emphasizing species-dependent disease responses.

column6: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Single-nucleus RNA sequencing profiled more than 80,000 nuclei from the prefrontal cortex of 48 people with differing burdens of Alzheimer's disease pathology. Analysis identified cell-type-specific expression changes and pathology-associated cellular subpopulations. Early changes were relatively specific to individual cell types, whereas later changes included shared stress responses. Sex-dependent transcriptional differences and recurrent alterations in myelination-related programs highlighted cellular heterogeneity in the response to Alzheimer's pathology.

column12: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of entorhinal cortex from six Alzheimer's disease cases and six controls resolved disease-associated expression changes across neural cell populations. APOE regulation differed among astrocyte, oligodendrocyte precursor and microglial subpopulations. Analysis of transcription factor networks linked these cellular states to disease-risk genes, including a lysosomal regulatory program in astrocytes. The study provided a regional reference for investigating cell-specific mechanisms of Alzheimer's disease.

column14: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Dynamic Organellar Maps combined subcellular fractionation with quantitative mass spectrometry to assign proteins to cellular compartments. A HeLa-cell resource integrated localization predictions with abundance estimates for more than 8,700 proteins. The method also detected redistribution of proteins after EGF stimulation. By distinguishing protein movement from changes in abundance, the study provided a scalable framework for investigating organelle composition and regulated intracellular trafficking.

column16: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Gene expression profiling and quantitative proteomics distinguished microglia from peripheral myeloid cells and other neural cell populations. The resulting signature included markers of microglial identity that were poorly maintained in established cell lines and were absent from recruited monocytes. Related features were detected in human microglia. Experiments with cultured cells and genetically altered mice implicated TGF-beta signaling in establishing and maintaining the characteristic microglial program.
column17: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Direct RNA sequencing characterized microglia from adult and aged mice and compared their expression profiles with whole brain and peripheral macrophages. The study defined a microglial sensome containing receptors and other proteins that detect environmental signals. Aging altered this repertoire, reducing some endogenous-ligand recognition programs while increasing microbial recognition and host-defense programs. Complementary protein and RNA assays supported the distinctive molecular identity of microglia.
column18: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Mapping RNA interactions of FUS/TLS showed extensive binding to nascent transcripts in mouse and human brain. Depletion experiments revealed broad effects on RNA abundance and splicing that were largely distinct from those caused by TDP-43 loss. A smaller shared group included long-intron transcripts important for neuronal function. Related changes in human neuronal models and ALS tissue supported a common contribution of impaired RNA processing to motor neuron vulnerability.

column20: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Proteomic analysis of postsynaptic density preparations from human neocortex identified 1,461 proteins. Linking these proteins to human genetics revealed associations with numerous neurological and psychiatric disorders. Evolutionary analysis showed strong conservation of the postsynaptic machinery across mammals, particularly for highly connected proteins. The study established a reference human synaptic proteome for examining how disease-associated mutations affect cognition, behavior and nervous system function.
column21: Abstract summary (paraphrased): TDP-43 binding sites were mapped across thousands of brain transcripts using CLIP-seq. Antisense-mediated depletion of TDP-43 in adult mice changed transcript abundance and splicing, including RNAs associated with neurodegenerative disease. Transcripts most sensitive to depletion often arose from genes with unusually long introns and functions at synapses. The work also identified a mechanism of TDP-43 autoregulation, connecting loss of this RNA-binding protein to disrupted neuronal RNA processing.

column23: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Affinity purification and mass spectrometry mapped a human autophagy network comprising 751 interactions and 409 candidate partner proteins. The network connected established autophagy machinery with proteins involved in membrane transport, phosphorylation and ubiquitin signaling. The six human LC3/GABARAP family members shared many binding partners. Follow-up RNA interference experiments showed that several newly identified components influence autophagosome formation or turnover, providing a resource for investigating cellular protein quality control.

column25: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens identified genes that modify production of dipeptide-repeat proteins from expanded C9ORF72 repeats. Follow-up work showed that the RNA helicase DDX3X binds repeat RNA and represses repeat-associated non-AUG translation. Increasing DDX3X reduced dipeptide-repeat protein levels and improved survival in patient-derived neurons. The study connected an unbiased reporter screen to mechanistic and disease-model validation of a regulator relevant to ALS and frontotemporal dementia.

column27: Abstract summary (paraphrased): A genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen identified genes controlling a GFP-PARKIN reporter expressed from the PARK2 promoter. Individual testing produced a set of positive and negative regulators. A transcriptional repressor network that included THAP11 restrained endogenous PARKIN expression. Removing this repression increased PARKIN-dependent mitochondrial damage signaling, including in induced neurons. The work established protein abundance as an important determinant of the mitophagy response.
column28: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Pooled CRISPR screens in human neuroglioma cells identified regulators of the autophagy receptor SQSTM1/p62 and recovered known autophagy and MTOR-pathway components. Comparisons with RNA interference demonstrated improved screening performance with CRISPR. Follow-up experiments linked disruption of the ufmylation pathway to altered endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and increased SQSTM1 expression. The study showed how reporter-based genetic screening can reveal both degradative and transcriptional control of a proteostasis factor.

column30: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Quantitative affinity purification mapped interaction partners of APP, presenilin-1, huntingtin, parkin and ataxin-1. Comparisons of wild-type and disease-associated variants identified interactions affected by pathogenic mutations. Follow-up assays and a fly toxicity screen supported the biological relevance of selected partners. The study linked an Alzheimer-associated APP variant to stronger interaction with LRPPRC and mitochondrial dysfunction, illustrating how differential interaction mapping can reveal disease mechanisms.

column32: Abstract summary (paraphrased): High-content RNA interference screens identified genes affecting recruitment of parkin to damaged mitochondria. Follow-up experiments established a role for TOMM7 in retaining PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane and identified opposing effects of HSPA1L and BAG4 on parkin recruitment. The study combined genome-wide screening, analysis of siRNA off-target effects and mechanistic validation to investigate early steps in mitochondrial quality control relevant to Parkinson disease.
column33: Abstract summary (paraphrased): An image-based genome-wide siRNA screen identified factors needed to deliver viral capsids to autophagosomes. Follow-up assays revealed substantial overlap with genes required for parkin-mediated removal of damaged mitochondria. Experiments on SMURF1 implicated its C2 domain in selective autophagy of viruses and mitochondria. The study connected pathogen clearance and mitochondrial quality control through shared cellular machinery while distinguishing these processes from starvation-induced autophagy.
column34: Abstract summary (paraphrased): Affinity purification and mass spectrometry identified proteins associated with TDP-43 in human cells. The interaction network connected TDP-43 to nuclear RNA splicing factors and cytoplasmic translation machinery, supporting roles in several stages of RNA metabolism. Follow-up experiments examined selected interactions and stress-granule localization. The work provided an early proteomic reference for investigating how an ALS- and frontotemporal dementia-associated RNA-binding protein participates in cellular RNA processing.
